p80.002: The blue man who lived in Europe did not build a great civilization on his own. But as he mixed with the descendants of Adam and then with the Andites who came in later, a strong stock arose that created a vigorous, forward-moving civilization. The Urantia Book explains that the white peoples of today were formed with the blue man at the center, mixed with several Sangik races, the Adamic stock, and the bloodlines of the Andonites and the Nodites.
p80.004: Long before the last Andites left the Euphrates valley, many Adamites entered Europe as adventurers, teachers, traders, and warriors. At that time the Mediterranean was still an enclosed lake, and around it the blue man from the north, the Saharans from the south, and the Nodites and Adamites from the east met. People from Mesopotamia had also been coming into Egypt for more than thirty thousand years, bringing art and culture with them.
p80.005: The Urantia Book explains that the Adamites mixed mainly with the blue man of Europe, who was close at hand, rather than with other races far away. The two peoples were drawn to each other, and among the people of this mixture arose vigorous and progressive groups called the Cro-Magnons. For this reason, almost all the waves of early Mesopotamian culture flowed into Europe, and this became the starting point of modern European civilization.
p80.007: Then great changes in climate and in the land took place. As the northern glaciers retreated, the winds that had brought rain moved northward, and the Sahara, once wide grasslands, slowly turned into desert. The people living there scattered in many directions: to central Africa, to Spain and southern Europe, to Arabia and India, and to the Nile valley and Palestine.
p80.008: At about the same time, the British Isles separated from the mainland, and an earthquake broke down the land at Gibraltar so that the waters of the Atlantic rushed in and the Mediterranean became a sea. This flood drowned dozens of settlements, and more people lost their lives in it than in any other flood in human history. Now that the western route was closed, Adam's descendants went north, around the Caspian Sea, and entered Europe from the east.
p80.010: Early European civilization after Adam was a blend of the blue man's energy and artistic gift with the creative imagination of the Adamites. The Cro-Magnon blue men were honest in their dealings and valued chastity. Both parents taught the children, and the children learned how to care for the caves, art, and flint making. They were brave hunters and excellent boat builders, but above all they were artists. The art of the blue man reached its peak about fifteen thousand years ago. Still, the religion of Europe stayed for a long time at a lower level than that of India or Egypt.
p80.011: Later the weather changed, and the wide grasslands of Europe were covered with forests, so people changed from hunters into herders, fishermen, and farmers. Culture took a step forward, but The Urantia Book explains that during this period the overall strength of the Cro-Magnons actually weakened. This went on until the last great waves of Mesopotamian people came in from the east.
p80.013: The Andites entered Europe in seven great waves, and the last group came on horseback. The first migrations of the Adamites were peaceful, but the Andites, mixed with the warlike Nodites, became a conquering people. The horse in particular allowed the Andites to move quickly, so they could travel far and still stay together, keeping their high culture.
p80.014: Until the Andite horsemen appeared in the sixth and seventh millenniums B.C., the world, apart from China and the Euphrates region, had made almost no progress for ten thousand years. The Andites who went west across the Russian plains mixed with the blue man and became one people, and they became the so-called Nordic race, the ancestors of the Scandinavians, the Germans, and the Anglo-Saxons.
p80.015: 5. The Andite Conquest of Northern Europe
p80.016: For three thousand years, the military center of the northern European Andites was in Denmark. From there, waves of conquest kept spreading out, and the Cro-Magnons resisted stubbornly for a long time. The decisive struggle took place in the valley of the Somme River in France. The blue men held out for more than five hundred years, but in the end they lost. Thor, who led this struggle, became a hero of the northern tribes and was later even worshiped as a god.
p80.017: The Urantia Book reports that during this conquest the blue man quickly disappeared through war and intermarriage. But the blue man's blood left toughness and vigor in the peoples of Europe, while their humor and imagination came from the Andites. By about 5000 B.C., the white races had settled throughout northern Europe.
p80.019: As the culture of Mesopotamia declined, the center of civilization moved to the Nile valley, that is, to Egypt. When the last great migration out of the Euphrates valley took place, the most skilled artists and craftsmen came to Egypt, and they greatly advanced the skill of working metals.
p80.020: The Egyptians gathered the gods of their many cities into one system of national gods, with a complicated theology and many priests. Some leaders tried to revive the old teachings of the Sethites, but their efforts did not last long. Egypt's first stone pyramid was built by Imhotep, an architectural genius of Andite descent. But as civil wars broke out along the Nile and outside tribes pushed in, Egypt's progress went backward for more than five hundred years.
p80.022: Even while Mesopotamian culture was declining, a high civilization carried on for a time on the islands of the eastern Mediterranean. Around 12,000 B.C. a tribe of Andites settled on the island of Crete. They were skilled in weaving, metals, pottery, plumbing, and stone building, and they could write. Later a group led by Sato, a descendant of Adamson, came to Greece and settled there. The Urantia Book explains that these were intellectually superior and beautiful people, and that the art and genius of the Greeks came from them.
p80.023: Greece and the Aegean linked Mesopotamia and Egypt and became the center of Western trade, art, and culture, and the Greeks became excellent teachers, artists, and traders who set up many outposts of culture in the west. Meanwhile, on Crete, the mother cult that honored Eve as the “⟦Q 80:7.7⟧great mother⟦/Q⟧” spread widely, and this tradition lasted a long time. But from around 6500 B.C., the spiritual heritage of the Andites declined greatly, and the world became spiritually poor.
p80.025: In the mountain regions of central Europe, descendants of the broad-headed Andonites had lived for a long time. The ancient Hittites also came from this stock. The Danubians, who moved north along the Danube River, were farmers and herders who made pottery and tilled the land. Through the influence of missionaries from Crete, they came to worship the mother, and they kept the funeral custom of burning the dead.
p80.027: By the end of the Andite migrations, the people of Europe were divided into three main white races: the Nordic race of the north, made up mainly of the blue man and the Andites; the Alpine race of the center, made up mainly of Andonites; and the Mediterranean race of the south, a mixture of Andites, blue men, and Saharans. Around this time the people of Europe also set up huge stones, like Stonehenge, to honor the sun.
p80.028: But The Urantia Book says that trying to divide the white peoples into these three groups is itself “⟦Q 80:9.15⟧a fallacy⟦/Q⟧”. So much blending has taken place that such distinctions can no longer be clearly made. Even in 3000 B.C., the old social groups were as mixed as the people of North America today. This story of countless peoples meeting, mixing, and building civilization together looks a lot like our own world today, where different people live side by side.
p81.002: When the missions of Caligastia and Adam failed, the plan to lift up the world was badly shaken. Even so, humankind did not stop; it kept moving forward. The text says, “⟦Q 81:0.1⟧Evolution can be delayed but it cannot be stopped.⟦/Q⟧” The violet race was smaller than planned, but the progress of civilization after the days of Adam was far greater than the progress made in almost a million years before that.
p81.004: For about thirty-five thousand years after Adam, the cradle of civilization was southwestern Asia, stretching from the Nile through Mesopotamia to Turkestan. The decisive force that made civilization take root here was climate. As the weather grew dry and game animals became scarce, people had no choice but to give up hunting and turn to herding and farming. Climate change did what no other effort had been able to do.
p81.005: At first, because farmers used many slaves, working the soil was looked down on, and the idea even arose that farming was a curse. But the text says that working the soil is really “⟦Q 81:1.4⟧the greatest of all blessings⟦/Q⟧”. Adam's descendants grew the improved wheat and barley they had inherited from the second garden and spread advanced farming skills, and as people came to eat grains, vegetables, and meat together, their health and strength also improved.
p81.007: Culture grows as the tools of civilization develop. Only when tools lighten people's labor can people do higher things. The first four great advances of human civilization were learning to use fire, taming animals, making captives into slaves, and individuals coming to own property. The origin of fire later turned into the myth of Prometheus stealing fire from heaven, but the desire to search honestly and fearlessly for true causes finally turned astrology into astronomy, alchemy into chemistry, and magic into medicine.
p81.008: Tamed animals became living tools for people and opened the way to farming and transportation. In particular, the Andites of Turkestan were the first to tame horses on a large scale. People lived in caves, then built huts of wood and stone, and finally made bricks and built houses. When a mud-plastered hut accidentally burned, people also learned how to bake clay to make pottery. The text says that by using powers such as fire, wind, water, and electricity, humans are more and more being set free from endless toil.
p81.010: Around 12,000 B.C., as the grasslands of Turkestan dried up, people had to find new ways to make a living. Some kept herds and farmed, but the more able Andites chose trade and manufacturing. In this way, starting about twelve thousand years ago, trading cities surrounded by farmland came into being. But the cities of that time were not clean; garbage and dirt piled up so much that the ground slowly rose.
p81.011: In this age, metals such as gold, copper, bronze, and iron were widely used. The person who made bronze by mixing copper and tin was an Adamsonite of Turkestan. The text says that traveling traders and explorers spread civilization even more than war or missionary work did. Trade brought different peoples together and helped cultures mix and grow.
p81.013: By the beginning of historic times, Eurasia, northern Africa, and the islands of the Pacific were full of people of mixed races. Originally there were five basic skeletal types on Urantia: the Andonic, the primary Sangik, the secondary Sangik, the Nodite, and the Adamic. But they have mixed so much that it is now hard to tell them clearly apart. Studying the bones of people today, we can only divide them roughly into three groups, Caucasoid, Mongoloid, and Negroid, and even these groups are mixed again in many places.
p81.015: The Urantia Book explains that Adam and Eve did not bring new skills, but that their descendants developed people's inborn abilities and hastened economic and industrial progress. Thanks to farming, domestic animals, and better homes, people were gradually freed from the hard struggle just to stay alive, and they began to look for things that made life enjoyable.
p81.016: The text says that cultural society is not a privileged club that anyone can join for free. Rather, it is like a company of workers striving to build a better world for their children to live in. People give up part of their own freedom to gain greater security, and society is a kind of insurance. Every right comes with a duty, and the text says that liberty with no restrictions at all is only a “⟦Q 81:5.7⟧vain and fanciful dream⟦/Q⟧”.
p81.018: Now there is no longer a source like the Andites to reawaken civilization, so the civilization we have must be carefully guarded and cultivated. The text lists many factors that hold civilization up: the natural environment and climate, material plenty that makes leisure possible, scientific knowledge, a suitable population, the ability to use resources wisely, language for sharing ideas, and machines and tools. The text says, “⟦Q 81:6.9⟧Knowledge is power⟦/Q⟧”, and explains that science sifts out error and cleanses religion of superstition. It also says that the hardship of machines taking away people's jobs, if it is wisely adjusted, will in the end free people for more worthwhile work.
p81.019: Especially important is passing the torch of culture on to the next generation. Insects are born with everything they need, but a human baby can do nothing without learning. That is why the home, play, and school are so important. The text worries that modern civilization has advanced greatly in science but has stood still in ethical awareness, spiritual development, and the protection of the home. The ideals of one generation set the path of the next, and just as no stream rises higher than its source, a civilization cannot rise higher than its ideals. The text says that if at first life was a struggle to survive, and now it is a struggle for a standard of living, next it will be a struggle “⟦Q 81:6.28⟧for quality of thinking⟦/Q⟧”.
p81.020: Besides these, other things are needed: specialists working well together, helping people find the right work, a willingness to cooperate, wise leaders, social change that is fearless but not hasty, and care not to collapse while passing from the old to the new. The text says that a high civilization is born when material wealth, intellectual greatness, moral worth, social wisdom, and cosmic insight come together. We are standing on the shoulders of those who came before us. To learn well what we have received, make it better, and pass it on to the next generation: that is our share of the torch.
p82.002: Marriage grew out of the fact that human beings are male and female. It is the institution people have built so that the two sexes can live together, and the home is the sum of everything gained along that long road. The text calls the home “⟦Q 82:0.1⟧the crowning glory of the whole long and arduous evolutionary struggle⟦/Q⟧”.
p82.003: Religion, society, and school are all needed for civilization, but the most important place where civilization is made is the home. A child learns most of what he or she needs for life from family and neighbors. People long ago did not have much culture, but they faithfully handed it down to the next generation through the home. The rich heritage we have received today must also be passed on wisely through the home.
p82.005: Men and women are very different in their natures, but the mating instinct has brought them together to have children. This instinct was at work long before people knew anything about love, devotion, or faithfulness in marriage. Seeking a mate is an inborn tendency, and marriage is what it grew into within society.
p82.006: The mating instinct is an amazing power that makes even a selfish person value children and the future of the race more than personal comfort. Yet when it is not controlled, no other urge brings so much harm and sorrow. So the text says that wisely managing this urge is the best test of whether a civilization is real, and it stresses that mankind always needs “⟦Q 82:1.10⟧Self-control, more and more self-control⟦/Q⟧”. Hiding things or acting like a hypocrite does not solve the problem.
p82.008: The history of marriage is also the history of how society, religion, and law have regulated sex. Nature cares only that the species goes on, and it leaves society to deal with the problems that result. That is why there has always been a struggle between instinct and growing morals.
p82.009: In very early times there were few rules, but once people began living in groups, rules and taboos about marriage appeared. These taboos were rough at first, but they brought order between men and women, and clothing, ornaments, and religious customs came out of them too. From them, little by little, ideas of vice and sin also grew. Women, however, were always bound by more taboos than men, and a married woman had to wear signs such as a certain hairstyle, a veil, or a ring.
p82.011: In primitive times marriage was a sign of being grown up and a way to gain social standing. Some tribes required a man to prove his courage before he could marry, and later a bride might be won through athletic contests or riddle contests. Sometimes a groom went to the bride's home and worked there for about a year to prove he was worthy. People of old thought it shameful not to marry, so they sometimes married off very young children, and they even married dead people to each other.
p82.012: Seen through today's eyes, many customs were strange or cruel. Some tribes made a widow die along with her dead husband or live in sorrow for the rest of her life. There was also trial marriage, to find out whether a couple could have children, and the text says this was not loose living but a serious attempt. It also points out that the modern attitude of marrying while planning to divorce if things go wrong is actually worse than the honest venture of our ancestors.
p82.014: Marriage has always been closely tied to property and to religion. The text says that property stabilized marriage and religion made it moral. Primitive marriage was more like a business deal than a matter of love, so parents and elders arranged it, and because of this, marriages long ago sometimes lasted longer than they do now.
p82.015: But in those times a woman was treated like the property of her father or her husband. A wife's unfaithfulness was seen as stealing her husband's property, and a woman's chastity became a condition for her father to get a good price. The text explains that even today's sexual jealousy is not inborn but grew out of these property customs.
p82.017: Little by little, primitive people learned that when they mated with people from another group instead of close relatives, their children were stronger and more gifted. So taboos arose against marriage between close relatives. Meanwhile, the custom of marrying within the family lasted a long time, to keep property or the secrets of a craft in the family, or to keep a royal bloodline pure. The text explains that these taboos came not from instinct but from society.
p82.018: In the end, the custom of marrying into other tribes spread widely. It lessened hatred between tribes, led to alliances, and became a foundation for building nations. The text says that outmarriage itself “⟦Q 82:5.9⟧was a peace promoter⟦/Q⟧”. Trade and adventure also helped people meet more widely and share their cultures.
p82.020: The text says that there are no pure races in the world today. Every race is already mixed with many others. The Urantia Book explains that when people of different backgrounds mix, new and more vigorous traits can appear, but the result depends on the backgrounds of the people who mix. It also says that most objections to race mixing come not from biology but from social and cultural prejudice, and that the hardships people of mixed race face are mainly caused by society's prejudice.
p82.021: Love and marriage are precious institutions that have been refined little by little over long ages. Learning to control our instincts, respecting one another as equal persons rather than as property, and looking at others without prejudice all prepare us for the better homes and society we will build in the future.
p83.002: This paper tells how the institution of marriage began and grew. Marriage started from loose relations among people living in herds, went through many changes, and at last reached pair marriage, in which one man and one woman build a home. Property and religion helped hold marriage up, but the real power that kept marriage and the home going to the end was the simple fact that men and women cannot get along without each other.
p83.003: The text says the sex urge was a hidden force that led selfish people to become more than animals. When people pair up, they naturally put themselves aside and take on responsibility for their family. In this way the urge made people think, and in the end it led them to love.
p83.005: Marriage is a device society has made to manage the countless relations between men and women. It regulates the sex relations of individuals, and it also sorts out family lines, inheritance, and social order. The text says that while marriages may be approved or disapproved from above, “⟦Q 83:1.4⟧they are hardly made in heaven⟦/Q⟧”. The family is a human institution that people have built, and religion should have a good influence on marriage but should not try to control it all by itself.
p83.006: In primitive times marriage was mainly for working together, and there was hardly any romantic love or free choice. Husband and wife grew fond of each other as they lived and worked together. But as civilization advances, marriage is becoming more and more caring, romantic, ethical, and idealistic.
p83.008: In primitive society parents chose their children's mates, later matchmakers appeared, and only quite recently has marriage become a choice made by the two people themselves. Long ago there was also marriage by capture, in which a bride was stolen from another tribe, and the custom of carrying the bride over the threshold is a leftover from those days.
p83.009: For a long time women could not decide their own marriages, but wise women always found clever ways around this limit, and as civilization advanced they took a bigger and bigger part in courtship and marriage. The importance of love, romance, and personal choice before marriage was a gift the Andites left to the world. Affection, instead of cold calculation, began to be the way to choose a lifelong partner.
p83.011: People of old believed that love and promises alone could not make a marriage last, so they used property as a guarantee. This is how the custom arose of a groom paying the bride's father a price to get a wife. A man without money might pay with work instead, or he might become the father's adopted son and marry that way.
p83.012: As civilization advanced, fathers did not like looking as if they were selling their daughters, and they began giving the couple valuable gifts equal to the price they had received. This became the bride's dowry. The dowry carried the meaning that the wife was no longer a slave or a piece of property but an independent person.
p83.014: The wedding ceremony came about because marriage was never just the business of two people but of the whole community. People long ago kept no written records, so many people had to witness a marriage. At first it was enough to announce that a couple would live together or to eat a meal together, but little by little weddings became grander ceremonies.
p83.015: People of old greatly feared being childless, so they used many charms and magic rites, hoping for happiness and many children. Throwing grain or rice at the newlyweds, the bride's wearing a veil, and the use of candles and water all came from customs meant to drive away or fool evil spirits. The wish that a marriage would not fail led people to seek out priests, and this led to today's church weddings.
p83.017: Early in the history of marriage, a woman's mating with only one man at a time was the first step away from herd life. After that came group marriage, in which several brothers married several sisters, and among more advanced tribes polygyny appeared, in which one man had several wives. Even under polygyny, one head wife usually ran the household.
p83.018: Women long ago aged early from frequent childbirth and hard work, so a wife would sometimes urge her husband to take a second wife. Rich men took many wives to have many children. The text says that human customs evolve, “⟦Q 83:5.15⟧but very slowly⟦/Q⟧”. It also tells of a chief who was persuaded to be content with one wife and sent his other wives away, only to be killed by their angry relatives.
p83.020: Monogamy, in which one man and one woman form a pair, is above all the best kind of marriage for children. It first arose because of poverty, but over time it came to have great cultural value. The text says that monogamy is always “⟦Q 83:6.6⟧the idealistic goal of human sex evolution⟦/Q⟧”. Because it calls for self-denial, it easily fails when people lack self-control, the highest of human virtues.
p83.021: Pair marriage nurtures fine feelings, mature character, and spiritual growth, and it builds the understanding and cooperation that are best for the happiness of parents and the welfare of children. At the same time, the text urges that people who do not reach such a marriage and live alone should always be treated with kindness and consideration.
p83.023: Long ago it was easy to end a marriage, and divorce happened mostly by the man's will alone. The bride price and dowry made people lose property when they parted, which greatly reduced divorce. Today, as people marry for love more than for property, marriage has become unstable for a while.
p83.024: The text says the real test of marriage is the close living together, day after day. When two people have been raised always to have their own way, it is hard for them to succeed in a lifelong partnership that needs give-and-take and devotion. It also points out that carrying too much fantasy and romance into courtship is a big reason divorce is increasing. So society should teach young people properly about marriage and prepare them for it.
p83.026: Marriage, which is completed in the home, is man's most exalted institution, but it is essentially a human institution. The text says it is a mistake to compare marriage to the relation between the Thought Adjuster (the spirit of God who lives in a person's mind) and a human being, or to divine unions. Even so, much spiritual growth can come when husband and wife sincerely strive together, and the text says the ideal mortal marriage “⟦Q 83:8.5⟧is humanly sacred⟦/Q⟧”.
p83.027: Marriage is one of the highest dreams people have. The text says we should not crush the beautiful dreams young people have about marriage, but before they marry they should also learn something of its realities. Today women more and more enjoy rights equal to men's, and the home is becoming a partnership in which husband and wife are faithful to each other and raise their children together. Dreaming of a good home while building self-control and consideration starting now is the first step toward making that dream come true.
p84.002: The text sums up the history of marriage this way. The need to make a living gave birth to marriage, the attraction between the sexes made it beautiful, religion approved and exalted it, and the state regulated it. And love, which grew later, made marriage shine as the root of the home, civilization's most useful and sublime institution. That is why the text says that home building should be the center of all education.
p84.003: Society is made up of families joined together. A person comes and goes in a short time, but the family goes on in society. The text calls the family “⟦Q 84:0.2⟧the channel through which the river of culture and knowledge flows from one generation to another⟦/Q⟧”.
p84.005: At first marriage did not arise because of sex. A woman needed a man's help to care for her children, and a man was drawn to the shelter where the women and children lived more by hunger than by love. Primitive people did not even understand well how babies came to be, and some believed a spirit or ghost entered a woman's body to make a baby. Only later did people learn that father and mother contribute equally to the life of a child.
p84.006: The very first form of the family was the relation between a mother and her child. A mother's love is not something learned from morals but an inborn instinct, and the longer a baby stays helpless, the stronger that love becomes. This mother-child relation was the seed from which marriage and the home grew. The home appeared only when the pairing of a man and a woman lasted long enough to raise children. The text says that a man and a woman working together are, in most ways, far better than two men or two women.
p84.008: The first family was the mother-family, centered on the mother. Because it was always certain who the mother was, family lines were traced through the mother. In those days the wife's mother held the greatest authority in the household, and the wife's brothers took more part in family matters than the husband did.
p84.009: But when people began raising livestock and men came to control the food supply, the mother-family quickly changed into the father-family, centered on the father. To establish the father's claim to the children, a strange custom even arose in which, when a wife gave birth, the husband lay in bed for days and received congratulations. The text says the change from the mother-family to the father-family was one of the greatest and most radical shifts mankind has ever gone through.
p84.011: In the age of herding, the father ruled his family almost as he pleased. Every society went through this stage of patriarchal authority. The Urantia Book explains that women were valued low long ago not only because of men's strength but also because, as mothers, they could not fight in times of war or crisis.
p84.012: Still, women always had to work, and for a long time it was women who actually produced the food. Women carried the loads, looked after the children, and grew the vegetables, while men hunted and fought. Woman's first liberation came when men began to share the work of tilling the soil. Because of this, women gained more time to care for the home and children, and men brought into farming the power of organization they had learned in hunting and war, greatly improving agriculture.
p84.014: The text says that in any age the status of woman is a measure of how far marriage has developed, and the development of marriage is a measure of the progress of civilization. Early woman was treated not as man's friend or companion but as property or a servant. Men did not understand women well and so feared or distrusted them, and many old stories blamed the world's troubles on women such as Eve or Pandora.
p84.015: People of old thought childbirth and menstruation were unclean and made many taboos that kept women apart. These ideas were foolish, but the text says they had an unexpected good side: they gave tired women time to rest. It was great progress when men lost the right to kill their wives at will and women became able to own property. Yet even today, in many places women have not gained full freedom.
p84.017: Nature is not fair; it makes women alone bear the pain of childbirth. The text says that only awakened morals and men's sense of fairness can make up for this disadvantage. The idea that men and women are equal does not exist in nature, but it is beautiful and valuable in civilization. Where might makes right, men dominate women, but as justice and peace grow, women are set free from bondage. So woman's status has moved in the opposite direction from how much a society values war.
p84.018: The text says that it was not religion but science that truly set women free. Once factories and machines appeared, men's strength no longer mattered so much. Today women have gained dignity, independence, equality, and education, and now they are being tested on how they will use this precious freedom. The text says that men and women each have their own proper spheres and rights, and that their differences will never disappear.
p84.019: 6. The Partnership of Man and Woman
p84.020: Men and women can never fully understand each other, because they naturally think and react differently. But the text says this difference is not a cause for worry; it is actually a great blessing to mankind. Woman has always been the moral standard-bearer and spiritual leader of mankind. Many beings in the universe are also made in two different forms like this, and together they overcome limits and do far more.
p84.021: Men and women need each other not only in this life but also after death, in the morontia career (the stage between material and spiritual life) and the spiritual career, and they will keep helping each other all through the long journey up to Paradise. The text calls marriage “⟦Q 84:6.8⟧the mother of all human institutions⟦/Q⟧” and says the family is man's greatest purely human achievement.
p84.023: When homes are good, society is good. The home in which one man and one woman live as partners began in the days of Dalamatia, and Adam and Eve were the first to show the world men and women working side by side in the Garden. Animals love their young, but civilized people love even their children's children and rejoice when their children do well.
p84.024: The text says that having children does not give parents rights; it lays on them the greatest responsibility of life. A child comes to respect his or her parents not because of the mere fact of being born, but because the parents care for, teach, and help the child with love. The home is the first school of brotherhood, where we learn patience, unselfishness, tolerance, and forbearance. The text says that society would greatly improve if homes were run like the family councils of the Andites, where everyone discussed things freely and openly.
p84.025: Above all, a good home helps parents understand how the Creator feels toward his children, and it gives children their first picture of the love of the Paradise Father. The love we receive at home is our first step in learning the love of God.
p84.027: The text says that the greatest threat to family life is today's excessive pursuit of pleasure. Enjoying ourselves is not bad in itself. Healthy play, rest, storytelling, and good food all have value, and the text says, “⟦Q 84:8.6⟧Let man enjoy himself⟦/Q⟧”. But the longings of the soul cannot be satisfied by bodily pleasures, and vanity and fashion cannot build a home or raise children.
p84.028: If pleasure tears down marriage and harms the home, its price is far too high. For the home is man's most precious achievement and civilization's only hope of survival. Enjoying life while controlling ourselves so that we do not lose what is more precious: that is the wisdom of building a good home.
p85.002: The first religion people had long, long ago did not begin with morals or spiritual teachings. The Urantia Book explains that it grew up naturally from biologic roots. Higher animals also feel fear, but because they do not imagine, they have no religion. Human beings created primitive religion through fear and imagination.
p85.003: At first, people worshiped the things of nature that they saw close by every day. They believed that every lake and tree, every waterfall and rain, had a nature spirit in charge of it. Strong natural forces such as storms, floods, earthquakes, volcanoes, and fire made a deep impression on people, and every happening they could not understand became something to worship. Even today we still call hard-to-explain events “⟦Q 85:0.4⟧acts of God⟦/Q⟧”, a trace of those times.
p85.005: The first thing evolving man worshiped was stones. Stones that suddenly showed up in a field, or rocks shaped like animals, seemed wondrous, and above all meteors, blazing as they fell across the sky, seemed like signs of spirits coming down to earth. In the Bible, Jacob also slept on a stone and poured oil on it. Almost every ancient tribe had its own sacred stones, and stones with holes in them were believed to heal disease. Even gravestones carry a trace of the old stone images.
p85.006: After stone worship came hill worship. Once people believed the gods lived on mountains, high places came to be thought holy. Caves, on the other hand, were thought to lead to an underground world where evil spirits lived.
p85.008: Plants were first feared, and then they came to be worshiped because of the drinks made from them. Primitive man thought the experience of being drunk was something holy. Sprouting grain also seemed mysterious.
p85.009: Tree worship is one of the oldest religions. All early marriages took place under trees, and people believed that some trees were home to kind spirits and others to cruel ones. The custom of finding underground water with a forked branch, the Maypole, the Christmas tree, and the superstition of knocking on wood all came down from this old tree worship. But long before such nature worship spread, the adjutant mind-spirits (spirit powers that help the human mind grow) were already awakening the very earliest worship.
p85.011: Primitive man felt a special closeness to animals. He admired their strength and cunning, and he thought their keen sense of smell and far-seeing eyes were signs of spirit guidance. Every animal has been worshiped by some people at some time, and beings that were half human and half animal were worshiped too.
p85.012: The Hebrews worshiped serpents until the days of King Hezekiah, and Chinese dragon worship is a leftover of serpent worship. People of old believed the wind came from the beating of birds' wings, so they feared winged creatures. The lamb became the chief sacrifice, and the dove became a symbol of peace and love. The Urantia Book says that symbols themselves are not wrong, but they must not be confused with idolatry, the worship of the object itself.
p85.014: People worshiped earth, air, water, and fire. They held springs and rivers in awe and easily imagined that spirits lived in bubbling springs and flowing rivers. Sometimes they would not save a drowning person for fear of angering the river god. Rainbows, wind, clouds, rain, and hail were also worshiped, and the same thing might be thought a good god in one place and an evil demon in another. Thunder sounded like the voice of an angry god.
p85.015: Fire was mixed up with magic. A person who believes in magic remembers for a long time the one time something worked by chance, but easily forgets the dozens of times it failed. Fire worship grew greatest in Persia, and even today candles are used in many religious ceremonies.
p85.017: Fear of the elements went on to the worship of the sun, moon, and stars as gods. In some places the stars were thought to be the glorified souls of great people who had died. Moon worship came first, and it was strongest in the hunting age. When the farming age came, sun worship took center place. Many peoples thought the sun was the ancestor of their kings, and they named the first day of the week after the sun.
p85.018: People also made up stories that the sun god sent a special baby to save the nation. They believed this baby would float down a river, be wondrously rescued, and grow up to become a deliverer who worked miracles.
p85.020: Having worshiped everything on earth and in the sky, people at last worshiped human beings as well. People of old did not clearly tell apart animals, humans, and gods. Anyone unusual was thought to be superhuman, and priests, kings, and prophets were worshiped too. Tribal chiefs became gods after they died.
p85.021: The Urantia Book says that, without the help of revelation, evolution alone never produced gods higher than the spirits of great human beings. In the words of the text, “⟦Q 85:6.3⟧Evolutionary religion creates its gods in the image and likeness of mortal man⟦/Q⟧”, but revealed religion seeks to change mortal man into the image of God. Nature gods and gods that came from human beings also blended together. Man worship reached its height when kings claimed to be descended from gods and demanded that their people worship them.
p85.022: 7. The Adjutants of Worship and Wisdom
p85.023: Nature worship seems to have arisen on its own in the mind of primitive man, and in fact it did. But all that time the sixth adjutant, the spirit of worship, was steadily awakening the urge to worship in the human mind. Even if the first worship began in fear and was aimed at objects in nature, the working of this spirit lay at its root. For primitive man there was hardly any difference between fearing, avoiding, respecting, and worshiping.
p85.024: Only when the urge to worship is guided by wisdom, the power to think deeply and learn from experience, does true religion begin to grow. When the seventh adjutant, the spirit of wisdom, is at work, people turn away from the objects of nature and turn toward God, the eternal Creator who made nature. It is good to remember that the urge to worship within us, too, is led to the true God when it meets with wisdom rather than fear.
p86.002: No special revelation was needed for religion to first appear and grow. It was enough for the human mind to work normally and for the sixth and seventh adjutant mind-spirits (the spirit of worship and the spirit of wisdom) to guide it. At first people feared the forces of nature, and as they came to think of nature as a person, then as having spirits, and at last served it as gods, that fear little by little turned into religion.
p86.003: 1. Chance: Good Luck and Bad Luck
p86.004: Besides the urge to worship, early religion grew out of the experience of good luck and bad luck. For primitive man, who lived by hunting, the results of the hunt were always different. People struggled not for a better life but just to survive, and fear of disaster that might strike at any moment overshadowed all their joy. When good things kept happening, they even feared it as a sign that a great misfortune was coming.
p86.005: The mind of primitive man swung between the wish to get something for nothing and the fear of getting nothing for all his effort. Life itself was a gamble. Later, when people herded animals and farmed, things such as droughts, floods, hail, and insect pests were all seen as good or bad luck. Even today, people's belief in chance and their attraction to gambling remain because of this ancient habit.
p86.007: Life was so hard that primitive man was always asking, “⟦Q 86:2.2⟧Who is tormenting me?⟦/Q⟧” When he could not find a material cause, he decided that spirits were doing it. In this way religion was born out of fear of the mysterious and awe of the unseen. When one thing happened after another, primitive man saw them as cause and effect, and he personified nature and chance as ghosts and spirits, and later as gods.
p86.008: The Urantia Book says that blaming everything hard to understand on supernatural causes is a lazy, easy way to avoid hard thinking. Words like luck and chance often really mean that we do not know the cause. As we keep exploring the happenings of life, we finally discover an orderly universe in which every effect has a definite cause, and then the fear of life is changed into the joy of living.
p86.010: Death was the greatest shock to evolving man. The Urantia Book explains that it was not the sacredness of life but the shock of death that stirred up fear and made religion grow. In primitive times people usually died by violence, so a natural death that came quietly felt all the more mysterious. It took a long time for people to realize that death is the natural end of life that comes to everyone.
p86.011: At first people believed that all sickness and death came from the influence of spirits. Realizing how weak they were before the great forces of nature and before sickness and death, people began to seek help from the unseen world.
p86.013: The idea that something remains after death began with dreams. When several members of a tribe dreamed of their dead chief at the same time, it was taken as proof that the chief had really come back. Breath, which looks like a cloud on a cold day, also caught people's attention, because breath was the sign that separated the living from the dead. From these ideas about dreams and breath came the most primitive idea of the soul: that a person is a double being made of body and breath, and that the breath that leaves the body is a ghost.
p86.014: The first idea of survival after death was different from a belief in living forever. People who could not count beyond twenty could not think about infinity or eternity, so they believed people were born again many times. Early man had no idea of hell or punishment, and he thought the next world was a place much like this one, only without bad luck. Only later were heaven and hell thought of separately, and each people pictured the destiny after death differently. The Egyptians' efforts to preserve dead bodies also came from such ideas.
p86.016: The invisible part of a person was called a ghost, a spirit, a shadow, and later a soul. To early man the soul was his other self in dreams. People believed the soul left the body at times such as fainting, sleep, coma, and death. Sneezing was thought to be the soul's failed attempt to escape, so people added words such as “⟦Q 86:5.9⟧God bless you!⟦/Q⟧” and they woke a sleeping person slowly to give the soul time to return. Moses forbade seeking God's will through dreams, and The Urantia Book says Moses was right, because the spirit world does not communicate with people through ordinary dreams.
p86.017: There were also many ideas about where the soul was located. Some peoples believed the soul was in the breath, the shadow, the reflection in water, the head, the heart, the blood, or the fat, and some believed a person had three or four souls. As civilization advances, these superstitious ideas of the soul disappear. Now, through revelation and personal religious experience, people learn that the soul is something created together by the God-knowing human mind and the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of God who lives within it.
p86.019: Man inherited a natural environment, built a social environment, and imagined a ghost environment. The Urantia Book explains that the state is a response to the natural environment, the home to the social environment, and the church to the imagined ghost environment. This imaginary spirit world had a strong influence on primitive society, and until revelation came, it was the only religion people had. Good luck was linked with good spirits, and bad luck with bad spirits. The Urantia Book also says that each generation laughs at the superstitions of its ancestors, yet repeats mistakes of its own that its descendants will laugh at.
p86.020: But an important change happened here. Once people believed that bad luck came when spirits were angry and good luck when they were pleased, they had to control their own behavior. This is when the idea of right and wrong was first born. Pouring so much effort into tombs, temples, and sacrifices to please the spirits was a great waste, but in the process people came to understand right and wrong, and human ethics was born.
p86.022: Primitive religion was a kind of insurance. To avoid bad luck, people paid expensive premiums of fear, superstition, and gifts to priests. Today insurance has become a matter of economics, and religion is rising to higher and higher levels. Even so, the old religion kept people from falling into despair. It made them believe they could do something to change their fate, and it made them aware that there is an unseen world above human destiny.
p86.023: The Urantia Book points out that people today are getting free of the mistake of blaming their misfortunes on ghosts, but they are falling into a similar mistake of blaming every inequality only on politics or society. Understanding the facts and acting wisely within natural law is the way to overcome so-called chance misfortunes. The fears of primitive religion plowed the soil of the human mind and prepared it for the coming of the Thought Adjuster. Ever since, the Adjuster has been working tirelessly to change the fear of God into the love of God. We too are invited to meet God not through fear but through love.
p87.002: The ghost cult grew out of the wish to ward off bad luck. Here a cult means a religious practice of serving some object with set ceremonies. Primitive religious rites were far from knowing and revering God; they were mostly attempts to avoid ghosts, drive them away, or force them to act. In a sense, they were insurance against disaster.
p87.003: The Urantia Book says there is nothing more pitiful than the picture of human beings living miserably bound by the fear of ghosts. Yet it was this very fear that led mankind onto the road where religion grows. Human imagination will keep moving forward without rest until it comes to know the true God.
p87.005: To primitive man, death was frightening because it meant one more ghost had been set free from a body. The most fearful time was after a person died and before the ghost left for the land of the dead. Primitive man thought ghosts had supernatural power but were not very smart, so he tried to fool them with many tricks. The Urantia Book points out that people today also often hope they can fool even the all-knowing God by putting on an outward show of piety.
p87.006: A house where someone had died was torn down or avoided. Because of this fear, sturdy houses and lasting villages were hard to build. People carried the body out through a hole in the wall instead of the door, came back from a funeral by a different road, and changed their clothes to fool the ghost. Mourning clothes, too, were first worn to hide the living.
p87.008: The first worship people offered was not awe but self-defense. They believed the living would be at ease only if the ghost left quickly for the land of the dead, and so funeral rites and funeral sermons came about. The funeral sermon was originally meant to teach the new ghost the way to go. Food and clothing for the journey were placed in the grave. People long ago mourned out of fear, but people today mourn out of respect and longing.
p87.009: The Urantia Book tells that because people tried to give a ghost everything it had wanted in life, there was even the dreadful custom of killing slaves or wives and sending them along with the dead. Breaking or burning tools and weapons to send with the dead was also a great waste. Civilization took a big step forward when paper models or pictures took the place of these things and property began to be handed down to the family. Because of a taboo against speaking the name of the dead, languages sometimes even lost words.
p87.011: The ghost cult led naturally to ancestor worship. Most of the early gods were glorified dead people. At first, ancestor worship was closer to fear than to worship. People even adopted children so that someone would offer sacrifices for them after they died.
p87.012: Most tribes held a yearly feast for all the souls of the dead. In Rome, it is said, about half the year was given over to such rites. People came to imagine that ghosts rose to higher and higher levels, and so ghost worship developed into spirit worship, and then into the worship of gods.
p87.014: At first people believed in only one kind of ghost. They thought good luck came when the ghost was pleased and bad luck when it was angry. Then the idea of two kinds of spirits, good spirits and bad spirits, arose separately in many places around the world. This idea explained both good luck and bad luck, and it led people to believe that spirits acted with some consistency rather than at random. The Urantia Book says this was a very important advance in the history of religion and philosophy.
p87.015: But the cost was great. The idea that good and evil fight against each other made it hard to imagine that the universe is unified. The Urantia Book tells us that when this idea first arose, there were actually no evil spirits in the world at all. Such spirits came only after the Caligastia rebellion, and even then only until Pentecost. Still, the idea of good and evil as equal powers has lasted to this day.
p87.017: Primitive man thought that spirits had only rights and no duties, while human beings had only duties and no rights. He blamed even the smallest misfortune on ghosts, and for fear of leaving out some god, he even offered sacrifices to the “⟦Q 87:5.1⟧unknown gods⟦/Q⟧”. He thought good spirits would do their work on their own, so he took more care to keep the evil spirits in a good mood.
p87.018: People believed that evil spirits envied human success and beauty and harmed people with the evil eye. So they gave children ugly names on purpose or waved off praise. Interestingly, these customs later developed into civilized modesty and courtesy. But under this cult, life became a gamble that depended not on effort or talent but on the favor of spirits, and endless rituals made life heavy. People tried to learn the will of the spirits through omens, divination, dreams, and astrology. The Urantia Book says that man is very slow to give up these outworn methods.
p87.020: Once people believed in good and evil spirits, religion went a step beyond avoiding bad luck and tried to force spirits to act so as to gain good luck. People used many ways to keep ghosts away, such as burying the body under stones or cremating it, and The Urantia Book explains that this is one origin of today's gravestones. They also shouted, rang bells and beat drums, or made frightening images to drive ghosts away. Water was thought to be the best protection, and this later developed into water rites such as baptism.
p87.021: Exorcism meant using one spirit to drive out another. People believed they could move spirits by vows and oaths, fasting, and inflicting pain on themselves, and so asceticism arose. People today still knock on wood or cross their fingers, and these, too, were once magic charms.
p87.023: Cults have lasted so long because they gave symbols that preserve and strengthen moral feelings and religious loyalty. Cults satisfied the emotions, but at the same time they were a great obstacle to social and spiritual progress. The Urantia Book says that a true cult cannot be made to order; it must grow. When a meaningless cult tries to overpower reason, religion becomes degraded.
p87.024: When the religion of Jesus is presented anew, new symbols will also be needed. Those symbols must be rooted in the idea that God is our Father and all people are brothers. The old cults were too self-centered, but the new cult must grow out of love put into practice. The Urantia Book calls the cult the skeleton around which true religion, the living personal spiritual experience, grows. Our worship and ceremonies, too, have true meaning when they come from love rather than fear.
p88.002: The belief that a spirit can enter and dwell in a stone, an animal, or a person is a very old idea that has been there since religion first began. This belief is called fetishism, and an object thought to be inhabited by a spirit is called a fetish. Primitive man revered not so much the fetish itself as the spirit he believed lived in it. At first people thought the ghosts of the dead dwelt in fetishes, but later they came to believe that higher spirits did.
p88.004: Primitive man made fetishes of things that looked unusual, and chance gave birth to many fetishes. If something happened while a person was sick and then he got well, that object became a fetish. The first fetishes were pebbles with unusual markings. Fire and water, trees and fruits, and animals also became fetishes, and eating an animal or plant that had become a fetish was forbidden. Thinking Friday or the number thirteen unlucky, and being unwilling to count livestock or people, came from the same root.
p88.005: The human body could also become a fetish. Spit, hair, nails, the navel cord, and such were held precious. People who were different from ordinary folk, or who had outstanding gifts, were thought to be fetish persons in whom spirits dwelt. Such people were honored as holy and even infallible, and in this way chiefs, kings, priests, and prophets came to hold enormous power.
p88.007: Ghosts were thought to like to stay in things they had used while alive. The custom of treasuring the bones or relics of saints and heroes grew out of this old fetish belief. Idols, too, are a more elaborate form of fetish. Moses tried to reduce fetish worship by adding the commandment against making graven images. This commandment helped cut down fetish worship, but it also held back the development of art.
p88.008: In time, words and writings became fetishes too, especially writings thought to be the word of God. The Urantia Book says this attitude turned the sacred books of many religions into prisons that lock up the spiritual imagination of man. When people believe that only what is written in a sacred book is true and that all truth is inside it, they will not accept even clear evidence. Opening a sacred book at random and making an important decision by the verse that catches your eye is also fetishism. Even so, going from fearing a chief's fingernails to respecting a book that holds moral wisdom sifted over long ages is real progress.
p88.010: Totemism is a mixture of social customs and religious rites. A clan respected a certain animal as if it were their ancestor, and this totem was both the symbol of the group and its god. Totems finally developed into today's national flags, the symbols of nations. Just as the old medicine man kept his medicine bag, the symbol of his power, from touching the ground, people today take care that the national flag does not touch the ground.
p88.011: Kings were said to rule by “⟦Q 88:3.4⟧divine right⟦/Q⟧”, and people have even revered the public opinion of democracy like a fetish. The Urantia Book points out that one person's opinion is thought to be worth little, but when many people come together, the same judgment is treated like a standard of justice.
p88.013: Today people solve the problems of the real environment with science. Primitive man tried to move his imagined spirit environment with magic. The purpose of magic was to know the future in advance and to influence the environment for good. Surprisingly, the purpose of science is the same. Through long experience, mankind has moved step by step from magic to science, and the fear and curiosity held in superstition later became the mother of scientific curiosity.
p88.014: Because primitive man did not understand natural death, he was strongly gripped by magic. When someone died, people thought another person had cast a spell, and innocent people were sometimes wrongly put to death. Fear itself could actually cause a person to die, and this made the false belief even stronger. When magic failed there was always an excuse, and the only remedy was more magic.
p88.016: Because people thought anything connected with the body could be used in magic, they carefully hid their hair, nails, spit, and even leftover food. This was not for cleanliness but for fear that an enemy would use these things to cast a spell. Animal claws and teeth, bones, and even the dust of a footprint became charms, and people believed that making an image of a person and handling it would affect the real person.
p88.017: Names were also very precious. A name was thought to be a power separate from the body, and it was sometimes pledged as security for a debt. This is like signing your name on a document today. Primitive man did not tell his real name to strangers and usually went by a nickname.
p88.019: Magic was practiced with wands, rituals, and incantations. There was public magic done by medicine men or priests for the whole tribe, and there was private magic meant to harm an enemy. The idea of good and evil spirits led to belief in white magic and black magic. Some incantations later developed into prayers, and magic dances were like prayers made with the body. Little by little, prayer took the place of magic.
p88.020: The Urantia Book calls magic a branch that grew out of the tree of evolutionary religion and bore the fruit of science. Astrology led to astronomy, the dream of changing metals led to metalworking skills, and belief in magic numbers led to mathematics. But a world full of charms also crushed human effort and initiative. Anyone who harvested more than others was suspected of having stolen his neighbor's grain by magic.
p88.021: Science is little by little removing the gambling element from life. But if education fails, people will quickly go back to the old beliefs in magic. The old magic was the cocoon in which science grew, but now it is no longer useful. The Urantia Book says that half the world is reaching toward the light of truth, while the other half is still held in the arms of superstition. Rather than relying on lucky objects or omens, may you be someone who learns the facts and reaches toward the truth.
p89.002: Primitive man thought he owed a debt to the spirits and had to pay it off. Over time, this idea developed into the doctrines of sin and salvation. Primitive man believed the spirits were satisfied by seeing human suffering and misery, and he thought he had to do something special to win the favor of the gods. The Urantia Book says that only advanced civilization recognizes a God who is always even-tempered and kind.
p89.004: A taboo means not doing something in order to avoid bad luck and keep from angering the spirits. Taboos first arose from chance experiences of bad luck, and later, gaining the authority of the spirits, they became a power that shaped laws and institutions. The Urantia Book explains that taboos were the beginning of human self-control and the oldest social rules.
p89.005: There were also many food taboos. Some peoples held the pig sacred and would not eat it, and others did the same with the cow. The Ten Commandments of the Hebrews also have the shape of the old taboos, “⟦Q 89:2.1⟧Thou shalt not⟦/Q⟧”, but they were a great liberation because they replaced thousands of outworn taboos, and they were new too because they promised blessings to those who kept them.
p89.007: Religion began with magic and ghosts and developed through spirits and fetishes into taboos. Every primitive tribe had its tree of forbidden fruit that always said, “⟦Q 89:2.1⟧Thou shalt not⟦/Q⟧” When people came to think of good and evil spirits, and taboos gained the authority of religion, the idea of sin was born. Sin at that time meant breaking a taboo, and death was thought to be the punishment for that sin. Sin was more a matter of outward actions than of the heart.
p89.008: The traditions of the Garden of Eden and Adam strengthened the belief that man began in a perfect state and then fell because of sin. When disaster came upon a community, it was seen as punishment for the tribe's sins, and because wicked people seemed to prosper, hell was imagined as a place to punish them. The ideas of confession and forgiveness also appeared early, but at first they were little more than meaningless rituals.
p89.010: The next stage was renunciation. People fasted, gave up many pleasures, and even sought poverty, thinking property a spiritual stumbling block. There were also practices of inflicting pain on the body. The Urantia Book says these things were often foolish, but they were valuable progress because they taught savages self-control. Self-denial and self-control were the greatest social gifts of early religion.
p89.011: The Urantia Book points out that the ascetic tradition of looking down on marriage and the home influenced many religions. The apostle Paul also held such ideas, but he himself made clear that they were his personal opinion, not a command. The Urantia Book says that marriage and the home are the true foundation of society. It also says that people must learn to enjoy liberty without license and pleasure without excess, and that self-control is better than extreme self-denial. Jesus did not teach these unreasonable ideas.
p89.013: Sacrifice did not come from just one root. Coming from the urge to bow before power and humble oneself before mystery, sacrifice was only one step away from the urge to worship. Primitive man measured the value of a sacrifice by how much it hurt. Early sacrifices included those given as gifts of thanks and those offered like paying a debt, and later the idea of offering something else as a substitute arose.
p89.014: As the doctrine of original sin spread, everyone was thought to begin life with a great debt to the spirits from birth. People offered their very best, and one Egyptian ruler boasted of offering an enormous number of sacrifices. In the end, people came to eat the bodies of the offerings themselves after the gods had enjoyed their souls, and this led to the sacred meal. The Urantia Book explains that today's forms of worship are also the old sacrifices of appeasement refined into ritual.
p89.016: The Urantia Book explains that long, long ago the custom of eating human flesh was widespread among the evolving races, and that at the time it was part of their social and religious customs. People thought the spirits wanted what they themselves ate, so they sometimes offered it as a sacrifice. The Urantia Book says this custom arose out of need and was kept up for a long time because of superstition and ignorance.
p89.017: This custom gradually disappeared through several stages. At first the eating was allowed only to a few, and at last it became taboo; this taboo began at Dalamatia, the old headquarters of the Planetary Prince, and slowly spread over the whole world. Later, animals took the place of human beings.
p89.019: The Urantia Book tells that human sacrifice, the offering of people as sacrifices, was once found among almost every people. It appeared as the eating of human flesh was declining, but it was a tragedy in itself. The Chaldeans gave it up early and offered animals instead, and one Japanese emperor had clay images used in place of people. Moses strictly forbade human sacrifice.
p89.020: Still, the old customs did not disappear easily. The Urantia Book gives the story of the Hebrew Jephthah, who made a foolish vow and lost his only daughter, as the saddest example of old religious customs clashing with advancing civilization. The old custom of offering a person in the foundation of a building has left its trace in today's ceremony of placing keepsakes in a cornerstone. The story of Abraham's being about to offer Isaac was also not a strange idea in that age.
p89.022: Moses tried to end human sacrifice by means of redemption. He made it possible to buy back, at a set price, land, property, or children that had been vowed as offerings. Groups that stopped sacrificing their firstborn sons became much stronger than neighbors who did not. The custom of putting blood on the doorposts and the custom of setting a baby afloat on the water also arose as human sacrifice grew weaker.
p89.023: The Urantia Book explains that an old custom, in which a woman who was to be sacrificed saved her life by giving lifelong sex service in a temple, spread into temple prostitution. The Urantia Book says such customs were allowed because morals always lagged behind the advance of civilization.
p89.025: Human sacrifice changed into milder and milder forms. Instead of offering a daughter, people had her vow lifelong virginity or tend the temple fire, and instead of the whole body, they offered a part of it, such as hair, nails, or blood. The Urantia Book explains that circumcision, too, first came from such partial sacrifice.
p89.026: At last sacrifice met with the idea of the covenant. Coming to believe that a god makes a covenant with man was a great step toward making religion stable. Law, that is, the covenant, took the place of luck, fear, and superstition. Only after man himself became trustworthy and moral could he imagine a trustworthy God. Yet early prayer was still closer to a bargain for health and wealth than to worship.
p89.028: Over long ages, human sacrifice changed into higher, symbolic rites. The old sacrificial rites led on to the sacrament of sharing bread and wine. The Urantia Book says that Paul may have burdened Christianity with his teachings about blood and sacrifice, but by teaching that Christ had become the last and complete sacrifice, he put an end once and for all to sacrifices of people or animals. Now salvation by blood has become, at least, symbolic.
p89.030: People of old could feel God's favor only through sacrifice. The Urantia Book says that sin needs to be newly defined. Sin is deliberate disloyalty to God. Guilt is the feeling of having broken a moral rule, but unless a person knows God and deliberately turns away, it is not true sin. Being able to feel guilt is actually a sign that a person is capable of greatness, and it is the first push to move higher through faith.
p89.031: Confessing sin is a brave denial of disloyalty, and it is essential to spiritual growth. God's forgiveness is the renewal of a relation of loyalty that had been broken. There is no need to struggle to earn this forgiveness; one only needs to realize and accept that the relation with God has been restored. When we make mistakes, turning our hearts back to God instead of hiding in fear: that is the joy of a forgiven child.
p90.002: Religious rites developed from the stage of avoiding and appeasing ghosts to the stage of sacrifice and atonement. As ideas about the spirit world grew more complicated, so did the rites, and in the end the rites were placed in the hands of medicine men, shamans, and priests. People came to believe that the gods did not listen to ordinary people but only to special persons. So someone always came between the religionist and the object of worship.
p90.003: The Urantia Book says that evolving religion is born of simple fear, but at last it reaches the realization that the Universal Father loves his children without limit, that is, all-powerful love. Between that beginning and that end came the long age of the shamans, who claimed to be go-betweens between man and God.
p90.005: The shaman was the chief medicine man and the one in charge of ceremonies. In many groups the shaman had greater authority than the war chief, and this was a sign that religion was beginning to rule the state. Long ago everything unusual was thought to be possessed by spirits, so people with unusual bodies or minds often became shamans. Many shamans believed they truly were possessed by spirits.
p90.006: But there were also many clever frauds. Shamans wore special clothes and used drugs, sleight of hand, ventriloquism, and other means to give people a mysterious impression. Because shamans were judged by results, those who failed at a task and could not give a believable excuse were driven out or lost their lives. So the honest shamans soon disappeared, and only skilled performers survived. Shamanism shifted the power to lead the tribe from the old and strong to the clever and farsighted.
p90.008: Shamans were in charge of tasks such as making rain, healing sickness, and finding criminals. They believed chance revealed the will of the spirits, so they made decisions by casting lots. Long ago, being chosen by lot could mean death, but now it only makes someone ‘it’ in a children's game. Omens, the stars, and the interpretation of dreams were also thought important. The Urantia Book says that even today many people believe they were born under a lucky or unlucky star.
p90.009: Shamans named babies, led funerals, and built up a reputation as the voice of God. They gathered great wealth from the gifts they received, became the first aristocracy free from all rules, and even put down rivals by accusing them of witchcraft. People feared shamans but did not love them. Yet in every age true prophets and teachers arose to rebuke and expose shamanism. The Urantia Book says that the respect people gave shamans also shows, in the end, how highly they valued wisdom.
p90.010: 3. The Shamanic Theory of Disease and Death
p90.011: Because primitive man believed that everything moved according to the moods of ghosts and spirits, religion also poured all its energy into material matters such as health and life. Since sickness and death were both thought to be spiritual matters, the shaman also came to act as a doctor. People thought about the causes of sickness and death in these stages. First they believed sickness came when a ghost lured away the soul, and so they feared and avoided the sick, which unexpectedly helped prevent the spread of contagious disease. Next, they saw injuries with clear causes, such as wounds from war or fights with animals, as natural.
p90.012: After that they believed sickness was caused by an enemy's magic or the evil eye, and because of this some people were wrongly accused as witches and killed. Still later they believed sickness was punishment for the sin of breaking a taboo, and The Urantia Book says this idea is still widespread today. Finally people came to realize that sickness has natural causes. The ancient Greeks were among the first to do so. The Urantia Book explains that evolution uses fear as a scaffolding for the idea of God, and when God is better known, that scaffolding is taken away.
p90.014: The religion of people long ago was also a way to prevent sickness. They firmly believed in their own treatments, and The Urantia Book says that this faith itself was a strong medicine. At first they feared the sick and abandoned them, so it was a great step toward humaneness when shamans began to care for the sick.
p90.015: Healing used methods such as singing and shouting, laying on of hands, and breathing on the patient, and little by little shamans also set bones, drained boils, and delivered babies. Water, sweating, hot springs, hot stones, and herbs were also used. The Greeks were the first to treat the sick by rational methods. The old remedies were kept secret, but The Urantia Book says that secrecy is an essential part of fraud and superstition, while only facts and truth welcome the light of understanding and scientific inquiry.
p90.017: Primitive man believed he could move the spirits only if the ritual was done exactly right. So the shamans gradually developed into priesthoods trained to perform rituals carefully. Rituals made customs sacred and kept myths alive, and in the end they developed into today's worship, such as prayers and hymns. But for tens of thousands of years, endless rituals also became a heavy burden on every part of life.
p90.018: Priests tried to fill people with awe through ancient languages and mysterious gestures, and The Urantia Book says the greatest danger is that ritual takes the place of religion itself. Priesthoods slowed down science and spiritual progress, but they did help stabilize civilization. And true religious leaders were priceless people who pointed to a higher and better way. What we can learn is to treasure the heart more than the form, and a direct meeting with God more than any go-between.
p91.002: Prayer was not religious from the very beginning. When primitive man became conscious of himself, he also became conscious of other beings, and from this prayer sprouted. Early prayers were not offered to a god; they were much like saying to a friend before some important undertaking, “⟦Q 91:0.2⟧Wish me luck.⟦/Q⟧” At first they were monologues, a kind of thinking out loud by oneself, and later they became ceremonies shared by the family and the tribe.
p91.003: When ideas of ghosts and spirits arose, these wishes were turned toward beings higher than humans, and as people became conscious of gods, they reached the stage of true prayer. In this early confusion, people prayed not only to gods but also to fetishes, ghosts, rulers, and even ordinary people.
p91.005: Early religion worked to preserve the precious social, moral, and spiritual values, and this was done mostly through prayer. Prayer was linked only with good purposes that society approved. So a person who wanted to harm someone had to rely on magic, not on prayer. In this way, from very early on, prayer became a strong force helping social and moral progress.
p91.006: But primitive man also asked in prayer for material things such as food and rain. This was a distortion of prayer, yet it also made people work harder to reach their goals. True prayer appears only when a person recognizes a personal being who helps him. The Urantia Book also says that the prayers of people bound by fear are in danger of sliding into excessive guilt.
p91.008: Prayer began as the putting of sincere wishes into words, became a way to gain the help of spirits, and at last came to help preserve everything of value. Prayer and magic have different roots. Prayer is always the active effort of the one who prays, but magic tries to manipulate outer reality while the person himself stays unchanged. When people learned that they could not force a god by prayer, prayer became petition, and the truest prayer became communion between man and his Maker.
p91.009: When the idea of offering sacrifices comes in, the power of prayer grows weaker, because people try to offer things instead of their own will to do God's will. And when a personal God disappears, prayer can hardly become true communion. Prayer also has the power to keep a person from becoming isolated.
p91.011: When young children learn to talk, they think out loud by themselves and sometimes talk with imaginary friends. Much of grown-up thinking, too, takes the form of a conversation inside the mind. Primitive prayer developed in a similar way, as a conversation with an imagined other self. This imagined partner grew from ghosts and fetishes to many gods, and at last to one God who holds the highest ideals.
p91.012: The Urantia Book explains that prayer leads a person in two directions. One leads to the storehouse of the unconscious, where experiences are stored, and the other to the borders of the superconscious, where one meets the Mystery Monitor, that is, the Thought Adjuster. So when you pray, it is good to think of the Father in Paradise, but a more practical way is to think of the other self who is close at hand. For the other self that was once imagined has now grown into the truth of the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of God who really lives within us. We can talk with him as if face to face.
p91.014: A prayer that seeks selfish gain over others cannot be ethical. The Urantia Book says that prayer must never take the place of action, and ethical prayer always stirs us to act. It also urges us to be fair when we pray, and not to wish that God would love us more than our friends, neighbors, or enemies. When we ask for forgiveness and for the wisdom of self-control, prayer becomes more ethical.
p91.015: Prayer that asks only for material things easily leads to disappointment once a person learns that the world runs by laws. But The Urantia Book says that even though prayer does not change God, great and lasting changes happen within the one who prays in faith. Prayer has fostered peace of mind, cheerfulness, courage, self-mastery, and fair-mindedness.
p91.017: The more the object of prayer becomes the highest and most divine being, the more a person's ideals rise to the divine level and the more the personality is unified and refined. Prayer offered together by many people is especially powerful. Praying together makes everyone who takes part better, and it can even renew a whole city or nation.
p91.018: The Urantia Book says that if you want to break the habit of criticizing some friend, the fastest and surest way is to make a habit of praying for that friend every day. It also says that the more spiritually enlightened should be patient and tolerant toward those who need symbols or rituals. The strong should not look down on the weak.
p91.020: Prayer does not directly change the physical environment. Prayer is not a technique for curing bodily disease, but it has greatly helped people enjoy health and has healed many ills of the mind and emotions. It has also turned complaining patients into patient people who give strength to others. Sincere prayer offered in faith is a strong force for personal happiness, self-control, social harmony, and moral and spiritual growth.
p91.021: The Urantia Book says not to be so lazy as to ask God to solve your difficulties for you. But while you bravely face your problems, never hesitate to ask for the wisdom and strength to guide and uphold you. As Jesus taught, we should pray honestly, unselfishly, fairly, and without doubting. The power of prayer has nothing to do with knowledge or position, and anyone can meet the Thought Adjuster within through prayer.
p91.023: Mysticism is a good way to sense that God is near. But it is dangerous when it draws a person away from others and slides into fanaticism. The Urantia Book says that contact with the Thought Adjuster happens more often while lovingly serving others than in quiet meditation. Jesus, too, withdrew with his apostles for short times of prayer, but kept them mostly in the service of the people. The human soul needs not only spiritual food but also spiritual exercise.
p91.024: We should not mistake every strong emotion or vivid feeling for a revelation from God. True spiritual ecstasy is usually very calm on the outside. To tell whether such an unusual experience is genuine, we can ask whether it makes body and mind healthier, whether it makes us faithful in everyday duties, whether it makes us love truth, beauty, and goodness more, and whether it makes us more deeply conscious of God.
p91.026: Primitive man prayed long before he clearly knew God. In desperate times he asked for help, and in happy times joy poured out of him on its own. The Urantia Book says that while magic tries to fit a god to man's conditions, prayer is the effort to fit a person's personality to the will of God. Prayer may be fearful submission, a merciful intercession for an enemy, a wish to change God, or a power that changes oneself.
p91.027: The Urantia Book compares it this way: even when the wind blows upward, a bird cannot fly unless it spreads its wings. Prayer is a way of riding the rising spiritual currents of the universe and lifting a person high. God answers prayer with greater truth, deeper beauty, and higher goodness. God responds not to words but to the attitude of the soul. The Urantia Book urges us to pray not for things but for values, not for satisfaction but for growth.
p91.029: The Urantia Book gives the conditions of effective prayer. We must face life's problems sincerely and bravely, and honestly make every human effort we can. We must surrender the longings of the heart to spiritual growth and choose God's will wholeheartedly, without hesitation. It is not enough to know and choose that will; we must actually do it, and we must ask for God's wisdom to work out life's problems. And above all, we must have living faith. If we pray today with this kind of heart, our prayer will become a true conversation with God.
